extracted.intended_audience: poets, aspiring writers, and literary critics (English-language)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for poets and critics on selecting subjects, constructing poetic action, and the aims and methods of criticism; emphasizes classical models, unity of action, and subordinating expression to moral impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of representation (interestingness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any accurate representation may therefore be expected to be interesting; what is not interesting is that which does not add to our knowledge of any kind; that which is vaguely conceived and loosely drawn; a representation which is general, indeterminate, and faint, instead of being particular, precise, and firm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle: we take pleasure in imitation because knowledge is agreeable; an accurate, particular, and precise representation gratifies natural interest. Avoid vague, general, or faint depictions — they fail to interest the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical enjoyment (art dedicated to joy)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is demanded ... that it shall inspirit and rejoice the reader: that it shall convey a charm, and infuse delight. 'All art,' says Schiller, 'is dedicated to joy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem must add to readers' happiness as well as their knowledge. Even in the most tragic situations enjoyment can subsist — tragedy often deepens enjoyment when the action is powerful. Aim to give delight, not merely accurate description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid depicting helpless, unrelieved suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations from which, though accurate, no poetical enjoyment can be derived: those in which the suffering finds no vent in action; in which a continuous state of mental distress is prolonged, unrelieved by incident, hope, or resistance; in which there is everything to be endured, nothing to be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such situations are morbid and monotonous rather than tragic; they produce pain rather than poetic pleasure. (Author cites his exclusion of 'Empedocles' on this ground.) Avoid scenes of unrelieved inward torment without incident or resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of an excellent action (subject selection paramount)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet has in the first place to select an excellent action; what actions are the most excellent? Those which most powerfully appeal to the great primary human affections: to those elementary feelings which subsist permanently in the race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select actions that move permanent, primary human passions — greatness and passion of action matter more than modernness or novelty. Classical examples (Achilles, Prometheus, Clytemnestra, Dido) show that ancient subjects can be more compelling than modern ones if the action is greater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must predominate over expression
rubrics_metrics.description: With the ancients the action predominated over the expression of it; with us, the expression predominates over the action. The poet should prefer his action to everything else; to treat it so as to permit its inherent excellences to develop themselves, without interruption from the intrusion of his personal peculiarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing works that exist merely for single brilliant lines or detached images. Subordinate rhetorical brilliance to the coherent development of the chosen action; efface the authorial self when it distracts from the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful construction and architectonic planning
rubrics_metrics.description: How different a way of thinking from this is ours! We have critics who direct attention merely to detached expressions. The Greek practice: Menander finished a comedy in his mind (constructed the action) before writing a single line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the action in the mind first; plan the plot and its development architectonically. Do not rely on accidental bursts of fine writing while neglecting the total-impression or structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability of subject to the kind of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: For all kinds of poetry alike there was one point on which they were rigidly exacting; the adaptability of the subject to the kind of poetry selected, and the careful construction of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects appropriate to the genre (tragic, comic, lyric). Some subjects suit grand tragedy; others belong to lighter forms. Misadapted subjects undermine poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and the one moral impression
rubrics_metrics.description: The all-importance of the choice of a subject; the necessity of accurate construction; and the subordinate character of expression ... the effect of the one moral impression left by a great action treated as a whole is unspeakably superior to the effect produced by the most striking single thought or by the happiest image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a single, profound moral or total-impression produced by the unified action. Emulate classical works that produce a calm, dominating effect rather than scattered brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, clearness of arrangement, and rigor of development
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearness of arrangement, rigor of development, simplicity of style — these may to a certain extent be learned: and these may, I am convinced, be learned best from the ancients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plainness and disciplined form over excessive curiosity of expression. Avoid over-tortured or artificially difficult language when it impairs comprehension (example: some of Shakespeare's passages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making one's private mental allegory the poetical aim
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is told 'a true allegory of the state of one's own mind in a representative history ... is perhaps the highest thing' — this view I believe to be completely false. An allegory of the state of one's own mind ... No great poetical work has ever been produced with such an aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conceive the highest poetic aim as an introspective allegory of your own mind. Such an aim tends to produce works defective as wholes (Faust is cited as containing such defects when judged strictly as a poetical work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not imitate expressive brilliance at the expense of fundamentals
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare's special gift of happy, abundant, and ingenious expression has misled imitators into reproducing expressive accessories alone, neglecting the fundamental excellences (choice of action, construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young writers risk being absorbed by attractive expressive mannerisms; avoid copying striking language while neglecting architectonic mastery. Use Shakespeare as inspiration but learn discipline from the ancients for method and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate on inward essentials rather than externals
rubrics_metrics.description: The externals of a past action ... he cannot know with the precision of a contemporary; but his business is with its essentials. His business is with their inward man; with their feelings and behavior in certain tragic situations, which engage their passions as men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating historical or distant subjects, focus on universal inner motives and passions rather than uncertain outward details. The date of an action is irrelevant to its poetical fitness if its essentials are powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of criticism: temper one-sidedness and perceive things as they are
rubrics_metrics.description: Political discussion ... in the hands of its express partisans is always likely to become violent and one-sided. This violence and one-sidedness Arnold believes it the work of criticism to temper ... 'of the literature of France and Germany ... the main effort ... has been a critical effort; the endeavor ... to see the object as in itself it really is.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should check fierceness and abstraction (the 'signal marks of Jacobinism') and aim to clarify and moderate. Cultivate critical discipline: it is a central literary activity that helps literature and writers see objects truly and improve standards.
